title: Progressive macular hypomelanosis (PMH)
summary: Ill-defined, non-scaly pale patches merging on the trunk of young adults. Think of it when ‘pityriasis versicolor’ has no scale and does not respond to antifungals.

glance.think: Poorly defined, non-scaly, symptom-free pale macules merging on the back and trunk of a teenager or young adult, often with darker skin.
glance.engine: Probably Cutibacterium acnes in the follicles producing a depigmenting factor. Melanin is reduced but melanocyte numbers are normal.
glance.backbone: Reassure. Options with variable evidence: benzoyl peroxide ± clindamycin, narrowband UVB, oral tetracycline.
glance.never_miss: Persistent, atypical, progressive patches in an adult may be hypopigmented mycosis fungoides. Refer.

what: PMH is an acquired, **benign** condition of ill-defined, **non-scaly** hypopigmented macules. They often merge into patches on the trunk. It is **asymptomatic**, with no itch, pain or preceding inflammation. It progresses slowly over years and may stabilise or improve after mid-life.
cause: The cause is not fully known. The leading hypothesis is **Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes** in the hair follicles producing a depigmenting factor. This is supported by **follicular red fluorescence** under a Wood’s lamp in many, but not all, patients. Genetic factors may contribute.
Melanin is reduced while melanocyte numbers are normal, and melanosome packaging is altered on electron microscopy.

list: Round or oval, **poorly bordered** pale macules that merge on the back and trunk, with or without the proximal limbs and neck.
**No scale.** This is the key difference from pityriasis versicolor.
**No preceding rash.** This is the key difference from post-inflammatory hypopigmentation.
More noticeable, and more often reported, in **darker skin**. Typically teens and young adults, possibly more common in women.
**Skin scrapings (KOH) are negative**, unlike pityriasis versicolor.
Dermoscopy shows ill-defined white macules with a faint pigment network. Biopsy is rarely needed.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: **Fine scale**; ‘spaghetti and meatballs’ on KOH; often yellow-green under Wood’s lamp
History of eczema, psoriasis or another rash at the same sites
Sharp, **chalk-white** patches, often on the hands, face and around orifices; bright white under Wood’s lamp
Faces of atopic children; mild scale
Persistent, atypical, progressive patches in an adult. **Refer**
Congenital, leaf-shaped; look for other features of tuberous sclerosis

list: **Reassure** that it is benign. Explain the *C. acnes* theory and the slow course.
Options with **variable evidence**: topical **benzoyl peroxide ± clindamycin**, **narrowband UVB** (specialist), oral **tetracyclines**, or combinations. Isotretinoin appears only in case reports.
Relapse after stopping treatment is common.
Refer to dermatology if the diagnosis is uncertain, or if the patient wants treatment for cosmetic reasons.

red_flags: Atypical, persistent or progressive patches in an adult: exclude **hypopigmented mycosis fungoides**.
Congenital or ash-leaf-shaped macules with other signs: consider **tuberous sclerosis**.
‘Pityriasis versicolor’ that does not respond to antifungals: re-check for scale and do KOH.
pearls: Do not keep treating it as ‘fungus’. If there is scale, take a **KOH scraping first**.
Photoprotection still helps even out skin tone.
Manage expectations: response is **slow and often incomplete**.
